narrative.overview:
The portfolio opens on Ivan’s identity inside a live GPU-rendered system. A fixed transparent WebGL canvas places a rotating wireframe topology core and orbiting data packets inside a long corridor. The first viewport contains no project imagery, so identity and technical authorship lead.

The corridor is the entrance to a connected spatial world: the project index is a System Atlas exposing all fourteen projects, individual projects are Evidence Rooms, About is a Career Constellation, Archive is a Technical Index, and utility routes are signal states. Shared geometry, atmospheric particles, pointer-responsive artifact frames, and spectral accents connect the routes without reducing them to one repeated template.

Ten projects use supplied interface screenshots. Four projects without original captures use bespoke conceptual covers that are explicitly labeled wherever they appear and never presented as shipped interface evidence. The system remains progressive enhancement: semantic DOM content, focus order, meaningful alternatives, reduced-motion behavior, and static fallbacks remain authoritative.
keyCharacteristics: Identity-first, project-free hero built around a live topology core and moving data packets.
Fixed Three.js canvas with scroll-smoothed camera travel through sixteen wireframe tunnel frames.
Three real project textures suspended as large planes with spectral wireframe echoes.
Semantic DOM copy remains above the canvas and owns navigation, reading order, alt text, and actions.
Mint, violet, and orange identify systems against a near-black fogged corridor.
One warm-paper manifesto and one warm-paper experience section reset the dark spatial journey.
CSS 3D hero and DOM project films form the complete static fallback.
Every major route has a specific visual role instead of reusing a generic card page.
All fourteen projects remain discoverable while real screenshots are prioritized as evidence.
Generated concept imagery is visibly labeled and separated from implementation proof.

rules.name: The Emitted-Signal Rule
rules.body: Mint, violet, and orange belong to light, linework, indices, particles, tags, and per-project identity; never spread them across large opaque backgrounds.

rules.name: The Interlude Rule
rules.body: Warm paper may fill a section only when the camera journey needs a deliberate editorial reset.

rules.name: The Identity-Scale Rule
rules.body: Ivan’s full name is the first display statement; WebGL motion supports it and never replaces it.

rules.name: The Two-Voice Rule
rules.body: Bahianita owns names and declarations. Manrope owns explanations, evidence, controls, and operational detail.

rules.name: The Camera-Path Rule
rules.body: Primary projects occupy distinct world coordinates and scroll anchors; never collapse the desktop corridor into a conventional card grid.

rules.name: The DOM-Authority Rule
rules.body: WebGL supplies atmosphere and project imagery, while the DOM remains the source of truth for text, links, image alternatives, focus order, and fallback presentation.

rules.name: The Real-Depth Rule
rules.body: Desktop depth comes from camera position, world coordinates, fog, occlusion, and project planes—not from a stack of shadowed DOM cards.

rules.name: The One-Artifact Rule
rules.body: Each stop elevates one real project texture; echoes and frames support it rather than introducing competing imagery.

rules.name: The Topology Rule
rules.body: Complex geometry expresses systems behavior in the hero; routine controls remain plain, rectilinear, and immediately recognizable.

dos: Do keep the first WebGL viewport free of project imagery so identity and topology establish the experience.
Do add the readiness class only after a renderer exists, and remove it on cleanup or context loss.
Do keep DOM project images mounted and hide them only while WebGL is ready.
Do preserve the complete CSS fallback below 821px, under reduced motion, and after WebGL failure.
Do dispose geometries, materials, maps, listeners, animation frames, and the renderer on unmount.
Do retain semantic headings, articles, lists, links, meaningful alt text, keyboard focus, and direct résumé/contact routes.
Do cap render cost and stop visible corridor rendering after the work journey.
donts: Don't describe or extend the CSS cube as the primary desktop hero; it is the resilience layer.
Don't place project imagery in the WebGL hero or reveal a project plane before its scroll stop.
Don't remove DOM content because the same project appears in WebGL.
Don't initialize WebGL for reduced-motion users or viewports narrower than 821px.
Don't use rounded cards, pill controls, opaque spectral backgrounds, or generic glass panels.
Don't let camera travel obscure actions, alter DOM reading order, or become required to understand the work.
